paragraphs.text: וַיִּשָּׂ֨א יַעֲקֹ֜ב עֵינָ֗יו וַיַּרְא֙ וְהִנֵּ֣ה עֵשָׂ֣ו בָּ֔א וְעִמּ֕וֹ אַרְבַּ֥ע מֵא֖וֹת אִ֑ישׁ וַיַּ֣חַץ אֶת־הַיְלָדִ֗ים עַל־לֵאָה֙ וְעַל־רָחֵ֔ל וְעַ֖ל שְׁתֵּ֥י הַשְּׁפָחֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esav was coming, and with him four hundred men. And he divided the children among Le'ah, and Rachel, and the two handmaids.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֧שֶׂם אֶת־הַשְּׁפָח֛וֹת וְאֶת־יַלְדֵיהֶ֖ן רִֽאשֹׁנָ֑ה וְאֶת־לֵאָ֤ה וִֽילָדֶ֙יהָ֙ אַחֲרֹנִ֔ים וְאֶת־רָחֵ֥ל וְאֶת־יוֹסֵ֖ף אַחֲרֹנִֽים׃

i18n.en: And he put the handmaids and their children foremost, and Le'ah and her children after, and Rachel and Yosef hindmost.

paragraphs.text: וְה֖וּא עָבַ֣ר לִפְנֵיהֶ֑ם וַיִּשְׁתַּ֤חוּ אַ֙רְצָה֙ שֶׁ֣בַע פְּעָמִ֔ים עַד־גִּשְׁתּ֖וֹ עַד־אָחִֽיו׃

i18n.en: And he himself passed over before them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֨רָץ עֵשָׂ֤ו לִקְרָאתוֹ֙ וַֽיְחַבְּקֵ֔הוּ וַיִּפֹּ֥ל עַל־צַוָּארָ֖ו וַׄיִּׄשָּׁׄקֵ֑ׄהׄוּׄ וַיִּבְכּֽוּ׃

i18n.en: And Esav ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yishaqehu* (וַׄיִּׄשָּׁׄקֵ֑ׄהׄוּׄ — *and he kissed him*) is the chapter's most narratively-loaded word, and the Masoretic text marks it with **puncta extraordinaria** — supralinear dots over each of the five consonantal letters of the verb. The Gen 33:4 dotting is the second of the four Genesis occurrences of the *nequdot* (after Gen 18:9 *elav*; before Gen 19:33 *u-v-qumah* and Gen 37:12 *et*) and one of the canonical fifteen *puncta extraordinaria* of the Hebrew Bible.

The **rabbinic-traditional reading** (recorded in *b. Sotah 13a*; *Genesis Rabbah 78:9*; *Avot d-Rabbi Nathan B 43*; *Pirkei d-Rabbi Eliezer 37*; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan; cited extensively in Rashi ad loc.) treats the dots as marking a hermeneutic reservation: *did Esav kiss Ya'aqov, or did he attempt to bite him?* The midrash exploits the consonantal-ambiguity of two verbs differing only by *q* / *kaf*: *va-yishaqehu* (root *n-sh-q*, *to kiss*) versus *va-yishokhehu* (root *n-sh-kh*, *to bite*). Two competing midrashic traditions: (i) Esav's kiss was genuine, and the dots flag the *exceptional* sincerity (the violent-hunter-brother here genuinely-reconciles); (ii) Esav meant to bite, but a miracle (Ya'aqov's neck turned to marble, in one version) prevented him, and the dots flag the *as-if-bite*.

The **modern text-critical reading** (Tov 2012; Yeivin 1980; Ginsburg 1897; Würthwein 1995) treats the dots as ancient editorial-doubt notation, marking textual uncertainty about the verb's authenticity in early manuscript-transmission. On this reading the dots are the ancient-equivalent of a footnote: *variant attested*.

The two readings are not strictly exclusive — the modern reading explains the dots' likely-origin (early textual uncertainty); the rabbinic reading explains their *received* hermeneutic-significance (the dotted-passages becoming sites-of-interpretive-attention precisely because they were marked).

The WoH translation renders *and he kissed him* (ASV-baseline; the consensus), preserves the dots in the Hebrew apparatus, and surfaces the kiss-or-bite tradition here in the commentary and in the central glossary entry `puncta-extraordinaria-v9-elav` (whose *appliesTo* is expanded in v2.31.0 to include this verse).

For the broader fifteen-puncta corpus and the standard scholarly treatment, see the glossary entry; for the Esav-reconciliation reading specifically: Sarna *JPS Genesis* p. 230; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* p. 526; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* p. 298; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* pp. 342-343; Alter *Five Books of Moses* p. 184.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשָּׂ֣א אֶת־עֵינָ֗יו וַיַּ֤רְא אֶת־הַנָּשִׁים֙ וְאֶת־הַיְלָדִ֔ים וַיֹּ֖אמֶר מִי־אֵ֣לֶּה לָּ֑ךְ וַיֹּאמַ֕ר הַיְלָדִ֕ים אֲשֶׁר־חָנַ֥ן אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶת־עַבְדֶּֽךָ׃

i18n.en: And he lifted up his eyes, and saw the women and the children; and said, Who are these with you? And he said, The children whom Elohim has graciously given your servant.

paragraphs.text: וַתִּגַּ֧שְׁןָ הַשְּׁפָח֛וֹת הֵ֥נָּה וְיַלְדֵיהֶ֖ן וַתִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶֽיןָ׃

i18n.en: Then the handmaids came near, they and their children, and they bowed themselves.

paragraphs.text: וַתִּגַּ֧שׁ גַּם־לֵאָ֛ה וִילָדֶ֖יהָ וַיִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֑וּ וְאַחַ֗ר נִגַּ֥שׁ יוֹסֵ֛ף וְרָחֵ֖ל וַיִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ׃

i18n.en: And Le'ah also and her children came near, and bowed themselves; and after came Yosef near and Rachel, and they bowed themselves.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר מִ֥י לְךָ֛ כָּל־הַמַּחֲנֶ֥ה הַזֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר פָּגָ֑שְׁתִּי וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לִמְצֹא־חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינֵ֥י אֲדֹנִֽי׃

i18n.en: And he said, What do you mean by all this company which I met? And he said, To find favor in the eyes of my lord.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר עֵשָׂ֖ו יֶשׁ־לִ֣י רָ֑ב אָחִ֕י יְהִ֥י לְךָ֖ אֲשֶׁר־לָֽךְ׃

i18n.en: And Esav said, I have enough, my brother; let what you have be your own.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יַעֲקֹ֗ב אַל־נָא֙ אִם־נָ֨א מָצָ֤אתִי חֵן֙ בְּעֵינֶ֔יךָ וְלָקַחְתָּ֥ מִנְחָתִ֖י מִיָּדִ֑י כִּ֣י עַל־כֵּ֞ן רָאִ֣יתִי פָנֶ֗יךָ כִּרְאֹ֛ת פְּנֵ֥י אֱלֹהִ֖ים וַתִּרְצֵֽנִי׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov said, No, I pray, if now I have found favor in your eyes, then receive my present from my hand; forasmuch as I have seen your face, as one sees the face of Elohim, and you have been pleased with me.

paragraphs.commentary:
The verse is the chapter's **structural keystone**. Ya'aqov's *ki al-ken ra'iti panekha kir'ot p'nei Elohim va-tirtzeni* — *forasmuch as I have seen your face, as one sees the face of Elohim, and you have been pleased with me* — explicitly echoes his Penuel-declaration at Gen 32:31: *ki-ra'iti Elohim panim el panim va-tinatzel nafshi* (*for I have seen Elohim face to face, and my life is preserved*). Three lexical-elements recur: (i) *ra'iti* (the same qal pf 1cs of *ra'ah*); (ii) *p'nei Elohim* (the same construct of *panim* + *Elohim*); (iii) *va-tirtzeni* (qal impf of *ratzah*, *to be pleased / to accept*), structurally parallel to 32:31's *va-tinatzel nafshi* — both verbs registering the surviving-of-a-mortally-dangerous-encounter from the encountering-party's perspective.

The chapter is staging the Esav-reunion as the **human-counterpart of the Penuel theophany**. Ya'aqov has just survived a face-to-face encounter with Elohim at night (Gen 32); he now survives a face-to-face encounter with Esav at dawn. The narrative-symmetry is the chapter's editorial-load-bearing feature: the divine-encounter and the human-reconciliation are framed as parallel survival-of-the-mortally-dangerous events. The reading is treated extensively in modern critical scholarship (Sarna *JPS Genesis* pp. 230-231; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* pp. 526-527; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* pp. 298-300; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* pp. 343-344; Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* pp. 219-222; Alter *Five Books of Moses* pp. 184-185 — *the simile is a way of saying that he has been afforded a glimpse of forgiveness in his brother's face*; von Rad *Genesis* OTL p. 325).

A philological note: a minority-reading (Speiser *AB Genesis* pp. 259-260) treats *kir'ot p'nei Elohim* as **polite-courtly-hyperbole** — *as one sees the face of a noble / a king* — reflecting the ANE court-language register in which an audience-with-a-king is described in deity-language; the *Elohim* would here carry its semantic-range as *judges / rulers* (cf. Exod 21:6; 22:7-8). The Speiser polite-hyperbole reading and the Sarna / Westermann / Alter structural-echo reading are not strictly-exclusive — the chapter could be doing both at once — and most modern commentators treat the structural-echo as the dominant register with the polite-hyperbole as a secondary-resonance. The WoH translation preserves *the face of Elohim* (capitalized, per WoH practice on *Elohim*), foregrounding the structural-echo without precluding the polite-hyperbole.

The central glossary entry `peniel-panim-el-panim-divine-face-encounter`, expanded in v2.31.0 to include this verse, documents the full *panim el panim* / *va-tinatzel nafshi* cross-corpus distribution and the Speiser-vs-Sarna philological debate.

The *minchati* (*my present*) of this verse is also the chapter's continuing-deployment of the *minchah*-vocabulary established at Gen 32:14, 19, 21, 22 (the four-fold gift-train) — covered by the central `minchah-tribute-gift-of-appeasement` entry. The v 11 substitution of *birkhati* for *minchati* is the chapter's next-vocabulary-pivot; see v 11's commentary.

paragraphs.text: קַח־נָ֤א אֶת־בִּרְכָתִי֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הֻבָ֣את לָ֔ךְ כִּֽי־חַנַּ֥נִי אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְכִ֣י יֶשׁ־לִי־כֹ֑ל וַיִּפְצַר־בּ֖וֹ וַיִּקָּֽח׃

i18n.en: Take, I pray you, my blessing that is brought to you; because Elohim has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough. And he urged him, and he took it.

paragraphs.commentary:
Ya'aqov calls his gift to Esav his ***birkhati*** (*my blessing*) — and not his *minchati* (*my present*), the vocabulary the chapter has been using since v 8 and that Gen 32:14, 19, 21, 22 established. The single-occurrence substitution is the chapter's most-deliberate lexical-recall: Ya'aqov, who twenty years earlier *took* Esav's *berakhah* by deception (Gen 27), now *offers* a *berakhah* at the reunion.

The Gen 27 narrative is saturated with the *berakhah*-vocabulary. The two structural-pivots: Gen 27:35 — Yitzchaq to Esav: *ba achikha b-mirmah va-yiqach birkhatekha* (*your brother came with deceit and has taken your blessing*); Gen 27:36 — Esav's lament: *v-hineh atah laqach birkhati* (*and behold, now he has taken away my blessing*). The exact noun *birkhati* (*my blessing*) of Esav's lament at 27:36 is the same noun Ya'aqov deploys here at 33:11 — now Ya'aqov speaking, naming the gift he offers Esav with the noun-form Esav had used to name the loss.

The gesture is **symbolic-restitution**, not legal-restitution. The patriarchal-succession-blessing of Gen 27:29 (*l'kha t'hi liv'om va-yishtachavu l'kha l'umim* — *let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you*) is not the kind of thing that can be returned-in-kind. What Ya'aqov returns is *property* representing the wealth-portion of the patriarchal-inheritance, lexically-named with the *berakhah*-vocabulary to recall the original theft. The verse closes with *va-yiftzar-bo va-yiqach* — *and he urged him, and he took it* — and the verb *laqach* (*to take*) at this closing echoes precisely the *laqach birkhatekha* of Gen 27:35: the same verb that recorded the theft now records the restitution-acceptance.

The reading is widely-attested in modern critical scholarship: Sarna *JPS Genesis* p. 231 (*Jacob's word for his 'gift' is *birkhati*, lit. 'my blessing.' The choice of word is deliberate, recalling the blessing that he had earlier wrested from his father in Esau's name*); Westermann *Genesis 12-36* pp. 527-528; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* p. 299; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* pp. 344-345; Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* pp. 219-220; Alter *Five Books of Moses* p. 184 (*the very word for the gift Jacob offers Esau is 'my blessing,' a sly hint of the blessing he stole from Esau*); von Rad *Genesis* OTL p. 325.

The paired clause *v-khi yesh-li khol* (*and because I have everything*) directly-parallels Esav's *yesh-li rav* (*I have abundance*, v 9). The two brothers' descriptions of their respective-prosperity are deliberately-paired: Esav says *rav* (*much*); Ya'aqov says *kol* (*all*).

The overlay glossary entry `birkhati-jacob-gift-as-blessing-restitution` documents the Gen 27 → Gen 33 thematic-recall in full.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר נִסְעָ֣ה וְנֵלֵ֑כָה וְאֵלְכָ֖ה לְנֶגְדֶּֽךָ׃

i18n.en: And he said, Let us take our journey, and let us go, and I will go before you.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֗יו אֲדֹנִ֤י יֹדֵ֙עַ֙ כִּֽי־הַיְלָדִ֣ים רַכִּ֔ים וְהַצֹּ֥אן וְהַבָּקָ֖ר עָל֣וֹת עָלָ֑י וּדְפָקוּם֙ י֣וֹם אֶחָ֔ד וָמֵ֖תוּ כָּל־הַצֹּֽאן׃

i18n.en: And he said to him, My lord knows that the children are tender, and that the flocks and herds with me have their young: and if they drive them hard one day, all the flocks will die.

paragraphs.text: יַעֲבָר־נָ֥א אֲדֹנִ֖י לִפְנֵ֣י עַבְדּ֑וֹ וַאֲנִ֞י אֶֽתְנָהֲלָ֣ה לְאִטִּ֗י לְרֶ֨גֶל הַמְּלָאכָ֤ה אֲשֶׁר־לְפָנַי֙ וּלְרֶ֣גֶל הַיְלָדִ֔ים עַ֛ד אֲשֶׁר־אָבֹ֥א אֶל־אֲדֹנִ֖י שֵׂעִֽירָה׃

i18n.en: Let my lord, I pray you, pass over before his servant: and I will lead on gently, according to the pace of the cattle that are before me and according to the pace of the children, until I come to my lord at Seir.

paragraphs.commentary:
Ya'aqov tells Esav he will follow at his slower pace to **Seir** (Edomite-territory, south-east of the Yabboq). But at v 17 he instead journeys to **Sukkot** (Trans-Jordanian, in the opposite-direction); at v 18 onward he proceeds across the Jordan to Shechem; and in the rest of the Genesis narrative he never goes to Seir at all. The two trajectories diverge at right-angles or greater.

The destinational-discrepancy is the chapter's most-noted editorial feature. Modern critical scholarship widely reads it as Ya'aqov's **continuing *aqav*-character deception** of Esav — the chapter's evidence that the Penuel-renaming (Gen 32:29: *lo Ya'aqov yeamer od shimkha ki im-Yisra'el* — *thy name shall be called no more Ya'aqov but Yisra'el*) has not fully-transformed the character. Ya'aqov has become *Yisra'el* in name, not yet in disposition.

The reading is documented across the major commentaries: Sarna *JPS Genesis* p. 231 (*Jacob's stated destination of Seir is a polite evasion; he has no intention of joining Esau there*); Westermann *Genesis 12-36* p. 528; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* pp. 299-300; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* pp. 345-346 (*Jacob's response is evasive; he never goes to Seir*); Speiser *AB Genesis* p. 260; Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* pp. 220-221; Alter *Five Books of Moses* p. 184 (*Jacob's speech to Esau here is in his old style of evasion ... he has no intention of joining Esau at Seir*); von Rad *Genesis* OTL p. 326.

The wider Ya'aqov-cycle deception-pattern provides the cross-narrative-frame: the *aqev*-grip and birthright-purchase (Gen 25:26-34); the stolen blessing (Gen 27); the selective-breeding stratagem against Lavan (Gen 30:37-43); the secret-departure from Lavan (Gen 31:20-21); the household-idol concealment (Gen 31:30-35). The v 14 promise to Seir, never fulfilled, is the cycle's final-deception-gesture and stands at the chapter's apparent-reconciliation surface like a thread left untied.

A minority-reading (Cassuto; some rabbinic tradition) treats the promise as polite-diplomatic-fiction that **Esav understands and accepts as such**. The reading is consistent with the courtly-protocol register of vv 5-15 but is less-prominent in modern critical scholarship, which tends to read the v 14 / v 17 discrepancy as deliberate-narrative-characterization.

The WoH translation preserves *until I come to my lord at Seir* (ASV-baseline); the discrepancy with v 17 is observable-by-cross-reference in the chapter-sequence rather than imposed-on-the-translation. The overlay glossary entry `ya-aqov-promised-seir-actual-sukkot-implicit-deception` documents the full reading.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר עֵשָׂ֔ו אַצִּֽיגָה־נָּ֣א עִמְּךָ֔ מִן־הָעָ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתִּ֑י וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ לָ֣מָּה זֶּ֔ה אֶמְצָא־חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינֵ֥י אֲדֹנִֽי׃

i18n.en: And Esav said, Let me now leave with you some of the people that are with me. And he said, What need is there? Let me find favor in the eyes of my lord.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּשָׁב֩ בַּיּ֨וֹם הַה֥וּא עֵשָׂ֛ו לְדַרְכּ֖וֹ שֵׂעִֽירָה׃

i18n.en: So Esav returned that day on his way to Seir.

paragraphs.text: וְיַעֲקֹב֙ נָסַ֣ע סֻכֹּ֔תָה וַיִּ֥בֶן ל֖וֹ בָּ֑יִת וּלְמִקְנֵ֙הוּ֙ עָשָׂ֣ה סֻכֹּ֔ת עַל־כֵּ֛ן קָרָ֥א שֵׁם־הַמָּק֖וֹם סֻכּֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov journeyed to Sukkot, and built him a house, and made booths for his cattle: therefore the name of the place is called Sukkot.

paragraphs.commentary:
The verse contains the in-text aetiology for the toponym **Sukkot** (סֻכּוֹת — *booths*), derived from the plural-form of *sukkah* (*booth, temporary shelter*). Ya'aqov *builds a house* (*bayit* — a permanent-structure) for himself, but *makes booths* (*sukkot*) for his cattle — and the place takes its name from the booths.

This is the **earliest HB occurrence** of both the toponym and the lexeme. The wider HB distribution: Exod 12:37 and 13:20 (the first stop of the Exodus from Egypt — the *Egyptian* Sukkot, geographically-distinct from this Trans-Jordanian site); Num 33:5-6 (the priestly itinerary version); Josh 13:27 (the Gadite tribal-allocation — the same Trans-Jordanian Sukkot as here); Judg 8:5-16 (Gid'on's confrontation with the men of Sukkot during the pursuit of Zevach and Tzalmuna' — the chapter pairs Sukkot with Penu'el, both Trans-Jordanian sites refusing Gid'on hospitality); 1 Kgs 7:46 / 2 Chr 4:17 (Shlomo's bronze-foundry between Sukkot and Tzartan); Ps 60:8 / 108:8 (the *emek Sukkot* / valley of Sukkot in the divine-warrior victory-psalm).

The **Sukkot pilgrimage-festival** (*chag ha-sukkot* — Lev 23:33-43; Deut 16:13-17; Num 29:12-38; Neh 8:13-18; Zech 14:16-19) — one of the three annual *shalosh regalim* — derives from the same *sukkah* lexeme. The seven-day booth-dwelling commemorates the Exodus wilderness-wandering (Lev 23:42-43) while also functioning as the autumn agricultural in-gathering festival (Deut 16:13). The Gen 33:17 occurrence is the lexeme's foundational-deployment, prior to the festival's legislation at Sinai.

The Trans-Jordanian *Sukkot* is identified archaeologically with **Tell Deir 'Allah** in the eastern Jordan valley (Franken 1969, 1992; van der Kooij 1989), a substantial Iron Age I-II settlement on the Yabboq's southern-bank-area. The site's most-famous find is the **Deir 'Allah Stele** (1967), an Aramaic inscription mentioning *Balaam son of Beor* (ca. 800 BCE) — paralleling the Num 22-24 material.

The verse stands at the chapter's **structural pivot**. Ya'aqov has just promised Esav (v 14) that he will come to Seir at his own pace; instead, at v 17, he turns north-west to Sukkot — in the opposite direction from Edomite-Seir. The two destinations belong to different sides of the Jordan-rift. The Sukkot-toponym therefore stands at the chapter's most-evidence-laden pivot for the v 14 / v 17 deception-reading (see v 14 commentary).

For the full cross-corpus distribution, the site-identification at Tell Deir 'Allah, and the connection to the Sukkot pilgrimage-festival, see the central glossary entry `sukkot-toponym-and-festival-etymology`.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹא֩ יַעֲקֹ֨ב שָׁלֵ֜ם עִ֣יר שְׁכֶ֗ם אֲשֶׁר֙ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ כְּנַ֔עַן בְּבֹא֖וֹ מִפַּדַּ֣ן אֲרָ֑ם וַיִּ֖חַן אֶת־פְּנֵ֥י הָעִֽיר׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov came in peace to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Kena'an, when he came from Paddan-Aram; and encamped before the city.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Shalem* (שָׁלֵם) is grammatically and semantically ambiguous and is one of the chapter's editorial-cruxes. Three readings are attested.

**Reading A — adverbial *in peace / safely / intact*.** The adjective *shalem* is read as a predicate-adverbial qualifying Ya'aqov's arrival. The reading is the dominant tradition (Targum Onqelos *b-shlim*; Rashi; ASV; NJPS *safe*; NRSV *safely*; NIV) and foregrounds the chapter's structural-resolution: Ya'aqov has survived Lavan (Gen 31), Penuel (Gen 32), and the Esav-reunion (Gen 33:1-16), and arrives *intact* in Kena'an. Modern critical commentators preferring the adverbial: Sarna *JPS Genesis* p. 232; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* p. 528; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* p. 300; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* p. 346.

**Reading B — toponym *Shalem*.** *Shalem* is read as a proper-noun place-name distinct from Shechem, giving *and Ya'aqov came to Shalem, a city of Shechem*. The reading is supported by the **LXX** (*kai elthen Iakōb eis Salēm polin Sikimōn*), the **Vulgate** (*et transivit in Salem urbem Sichimorum*), and the **Peshitta**. The Shechem-area Shalem-toponym is attested archaeologically at Tell Salim (modern Salem), a small village ca. 6 km east of Nablus. This Shalem is distinct from the **Yerushalayim-Shalem** of Gen 14:18 (*Malkitzedek melekh Shalem*; cf. Ps 76:3). The toponym-reading is favored by Hamilton *NICOT* p. 346 as a serious option; B. Mazar *The Early Biblical Period* supports the Tell-Salim identification.

**Reading C — in-text wordplay (both-at-once).** *Shalem* combines with the chapter's prior Penuel-and-reunion narrative as a deliberate wordplay: Ya'aqov who *strove with Elohim* (*Yisra'el* — Gen 32:29) and survived now arrives *whole / at peace* (*shalem*). The reading is preferred by Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* p. 222 and Alter *Five Books of Moses* p. 185 (*Jacob came whole to the city of Shechem* — *given Jacob's recent wrestling-injury and the high-anxiety meeting with his brother, the word resonates richly*). The wordplay-reading is editorially-attractive because the chapter's prior *yesh-li rav* / *yesh-li khol* vocabulary (vv 9, 11) clusters with the *shalem* / *shalom* root.

The three readings are not strictly-exclusive — many commentators treat them as overlapping. The WoH translation renders *in peace* (ASV-baseline, the dominant tradition); the toponym and wordplay alternatives are documented as defensible readings. For full treatment: the overlay glossary entry `shalem-shechem-arrival-three-readings`.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּ֜קֶן אֶת־חֶלְקַ֣ת הַשָּׂדֶ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָֽטָה־שָׁם֙ אָהֳל֔וֹ מִיַּ֥ד בְּנֵֽי־חֲמ֖וֹר אֲבִ֣י שְׁכֶ֑ם בְּמֵאָ֖ה קְשִׂיטָֽה׃

i18n.en: And he bought the parcel of ground, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the sons of Chamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred kesitah.

paragraphs.commentary:
Three converging editorial features at this verse.

**(a) The patriarchal-land-acquisition pattern.** The verse stages the second of three HB patriarchal-period land-purchases that together establish the foundational HB **legal-title-establishment** motif: Gen 23 (Avraham at Makhpelah, from Efron and the *bnei Het* / Hittites, for four hundred shekels of silver — burial-cave); **Gen 33:19** (here — Ya'aqov at Shechem, from the *bnei Chamor* / Hivites, for one hundred kesitah — encampment-and-altar-site); Josh 24:32 (the legal-conclusion — Yosef's bones buried at this same parcel: *b-chelqat ha-sadeh asher qanah Ya'aqov me'et b'nei-Chamor avi Shechem b-me'ah kesitah* — *in the parcel of ground which Ya'aqov bought from the sons of Chamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred kesitah*). The three verses share a distinctive legal-formal vocabulary: the *qanah* verb, the *mi-yad / me'et* preposition (*from the hand of / from*), the named-witnesses, and the explicit money-payment. The pattern looks forward to 2 Sam 24:24 (David's purchase of Aravnah's threshing-floor for fifty shekels of silver, the future Temple-site), extending the *acquisition-by-purchase* legal-title-mode from patriarchal-period to monarchic-period.

**(b) The Hivite-not-Hittite distinction.** The *bnei Chamor* are identified at Gen 34:2 as **Hivites** (*Shechem ben-Chamor ha-Chivvi*) — **not** Hittites. The Hivites and Hittites are listed as distinct peoples across the Canaanite-ten-nations-lists (Gen 10:15-17; Exod 3:8, 17; 23:23; 33:2; 34:11; Deut 7:1; 20:17; Josh 9:1; 11:3; 12:8; 24:11; Judg 3:5; 1 Kgs 9:20; etc.). The existing central glossary entry `bnei-het-hittites-canaanite-anatolian-question` (covering Gen 23) is therefore **not** cross-applied to this verse. The two-people distinction is editorially-significant: Avraham's southern-purchase is from the Hittites at Hevron; Ya'aqov's central-purchase is from the Hivites at Shechem. The Hivites' ethnographic-identity is itself debated in modern critical scholarship — Speiser *AB Genesis* pp. 263-264 favors a Hurrian-identification (the LXX sometimes renders *Chivvi* as *Chorraios* / *Horite*); Sarna *JPS Genesis* p. 233 and Westermann *Genesis 12-36* pp. 528-529 review the difficulty without committing. The WoH translation preserves the MT designations without ethnographic-identification.

**(c) The kesitah unit.** The payment-amount is **one hundred kesitah** — an archaic Hebrew unit of currency or weight, occurring only at Gen 33:19, Josh 24:32, and Job 42:11. The unit's value is unknown; the HB never specifies an exchange-rate with the shekel-system. The LXX renders *kesitah* as *amnados* (lamb) at Gen 33:19 and *amnoi* (lambs) at Josh 24:32 — possibly reflecting an early tradition of lamb-shaped weights or lamb-equivalent-value. Modern philology does not endorse the lamb-identification. The WoH translation preserves *kesitah* untranslated, following the central glossary entry `kesitah`.

**Forward-link to Josh 24.** The Shechem-parcel is forward-linked to Josh 24:32 (Yosef's bones) and to Josh 24:1-28 (Yehoshua's covenant-renewal at Shechem in the people of Yisra'el's name). Shechem becomes a foundational-covenantal-site at the *entrance* of the patriarchal-period (Gen 33:19-20) and at the *exit* of the conquest-period (Josh 24).

For the full cross-corpus pattern, the ANE-comparative legal-formulae, and the Hivite-identification literature, see the central glossary entry `patriarchal-land-acquisition-pattern-makhpelah-shechem` (new in v2.31.0).

paragraphs.text: וַיַּצֶּב־שָׁ֖ם מִזְבֵּ֑חַ וַיִּ֨קְרָא־ל֔וֹ אֵ֖ל אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ (ס)

i18n.en: And he erected there an altar, and called it El Elohei Yisra'el.

paragraphs.commentary:
The chapter closes with the **first explicit divine-name application** of Ya'aqov's new name *Yisra'el*: ***El Elohei Yisra'el*** — *El, the Elohim of Yisra'el*. The compound is the **fifth and final patriarchal El-compound** in the Genesis cycle, completing a pattern initiated at Gen 14 and developed across the Avraham and Yitzchaq cycles:

- (i) **El Elyon** — Gen 14:18-22 (Avram and Melchizedek at Salem)
- (ii) **El Ro'i** — Gen 16:13 (Hagar at the wilderness-spring)
- (iii) **El Shaddai** — Gen 17:1 (Avraham, covenant-of-circumcision; subsequently 28:3, 35:11, 43:14, 48:3, 49:25)
- (iv) **YHWH El Olam** — Gen 21:33 (Avraham at Be'er Sheva)
- (v) **El Elohei Yisra'el** — Gen 33:20 (here — Ya'aqov / Yisra'el at Shechem)

The compound's grammatical structure is distinctive: *El* (the West-Semitic high-god-name, head-noun) + *Elohei* (construct-form of *Elohim*) + *Yisra'el* (the proper-noun of Ya'aqov's new name, itself containing the *El*-element by the v 29 aetiology *sarita im-Elohim*). The compound is a **double-divine-name + theophoric-personal-name** construction — *El who is the Elohim of (the patriarch) Yisra'el*.

The verse stands at a **lexical hinge**. *Yisra'el* here is the personal name of Ya'aqov (the renaming at Gen 32:29; reconfirmed at Gen 35:10) — but the compound *Elohei Yisra'el* will subsequently become the **collective-name of the deity-of-the-people** across the HB. The first explicit-collective deployment is Exod 5:1: *koh-amar YHWH Elohei Yisra'el shalach et-ami* — *thus says YHWH, the Elohim of Yisra'el, send my people away* — where *Yisra'el* unambiguously refers to the people. The formula recurs hundreds of times across the HB (Pentateuch, Former and Latter Prophets, Psalms, Chronicles); Gen 33:20 is its lexical-foundation in the patriarchal-individual-register before the collective-people register opens.

The modern critical reading of the patriarchal El-compound pattern derives from **A. Alt** *Der Gott der Väter* (1929) and is canonically developed in **F. M. Cross** *Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic* (1973) ch. 1. The El-compounds preserve the **pre-Israelite West-Semitic El-religion** as locally-diversified across the patriarchal sanctuary-sites, with each compound corresponding to that site's specific local El-cult; the Yahwistic-editor harmonizes each compound with YHWH through appositional constructions (*YHWH El Elyon* Gen 14:22; *YHWH El Olam* Gen 21:33; implicit elsewhere) to produce the canonical text's monotheistic *YHWH = the El of each site*. For Shechem specifically, the **temple of El-berit** at Judg 9:46 preserves an El-compound name that continues the patriarchal pattern into the Iron Age; the Ugaritic material documents a parallel West-Semitic El-religion in the late-Bronze-Age (Cross 1973; Smith *The Origins of Biblical Monotheism* 2001; Day *Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan* 2000).

The altar-erection-and-naming sequence parallels the prior patriarchal cultic-site-establishments: Gen 12:7 (Avram at Shechem); Gen 12:8 (Avram at Beit-El); Gen 13:18 (Avram at Mamre); Gen 22:9 (Avraham at the Aqedah-site); Gen 26:25 (Yitzchaq at Be'er Sheva); Gen 35:7 (Ya'aqov at Beit-El). The Gen 33:20 altar is **the first altar Ya'aqov erects** in the Kena'an-return.

The Shechem-altar is forward-linked to Josh 24 (Yehoshua's covenant-renewal at Shechem in the people of Yisra'el's name) — establishing Shechem as a structural-bookend at the *entrance* of the patriarchal-period and the *exit* of the conquest-period.

The WoH translation renders *El Elohei Yisra'el* (transliterated, unhyphenated), matching the WoH El-compound practice across *El Elyon*, *El Ro'i*, *El Shaddai*, *YHWH El Olam*. The collapsed-to-English rendering *God, the God of Israel* (NIV) discards the El-compound and is rejected per WoH practice.
